gecko.e: The modern form was probably borrowed into English and other European languages from Dutch gekko (1718). Contemporary English forms were chacco (1711) and jackoa (1724). The further origin is not quite clear. Some sources mention a supposed Malay gekok, gekoq, or gekop, which would be imitative of the gecko’s chirping sound.
gecko.g: Any lizard in the infraorder Gekkota.

gem.e: From Middle English gemme, gimme, yimme, ȝimme, from Old English ġimm, from Proto-West Germanic *gimmu (“gem”) and Old French gemme (“gem”), both from Latin gemma (“a swelling bud; jewel, gem”).
gem.g: A precious stone, usually of substantial monetary value or prized for its beauty or shine.

gemstone.e: From Middle English gimstone, alteration (due to Middle English gemme) of earlier ȝimston, ȝimstan, from Old English ġimstān, ġymstān (“gem; jewel; precious stone”), equivalent to gem + stone.
gemstone.g: A gem, usually made of minerals.

gender.e: From Middle English gendre, borrowed from Old French gendre, borrowed from Latin genere (“type, kind”). The verb developed after the noun.
From Middle English gendren, from Middle French gendrer, from Latin generāre.

genealogical.e: From French généalogique + -al, equivalent to genealogy + -ical.

genealogy.e: From Middle English genealogie, genologie, genelogie, from Old French genealogie (Modern French généalogie), from Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”), equivalent to Ancient Greek γενεά (geneá) + -logy.
genealogy.g: The descent of a person, family, or group from an ancestor or ancestors; lineage or pedigree.

general.e: From Middle English general, in turn from Anglo-Norman general, generall, Middle French general, and their source, Latin generālis, from genus (“class, kind”) + -ālis (“-al”).
general.g: Including or involving every part or member of a given or implied entity, whole, etc.; common to all, universal.

generally.e: From Middle English generally, generalliche, equivalent to general + -ly.

generate.e: From Latin generō (“beget, procreate, produce”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from genus (“a kind, race, family”, gener- in compounds) + -ō; see genus.
generate.g: To bring into being; give rise to.

generate.e: Borrowed from Latin generātus, perfect passive participle of generō (“beget, procreate, produce”).

generation.e: From Middle English generacioun, from Old French generacion, and its etymon Latin generātiō, from generāre (“to beget, generate”). By surface analysis, generate + -ion.
generation.g: The act of creating something or bringing something into being; production, creation.

generosity.e: From Middle English generosite, from Latin generōsitās, equivalent to generous + -ity.
generosity.g: The trait of being willing to donate money, resources, or time.

generous.e: From Middle French genereux, and its source, Latin generōsus (“of noble birth”), from genus (“race, stock”).
generous.g: Noble in behaviour or actions; principled, not petty; kind, magnanimous.

gentle.e: From Middle English gentil (“courteous, noble”), from Old French gentil (“high-born, noble”), from Latin gentilis (“of the same family or clan”), from gens (“ clan”).
gentle.g: Tender and amiable; of a considerate or kindly disposition.

gentleness.e: From Middle English gentilnesse; equivalent to gentle + -ness.

gently.e: From Middle English gentilly, gentlych, gentilliche, equivalent to gentle + -ly, with *-lely simplified to -ly by haplology.
gently.g: In a manner characterized by gentleness

genuine.g: Belonging to, or proceeding from the original stock; native.

gerah.e: From Hebrew גֵּרָה (gerá, “twentieth of a shekel”, literally “cud”).
gerah.g: An ancient Hebrew unit of weight and currency, one twentieth of a shekel.

get.e: From Middle English geten, from Old Norse geta, from Proto-Germanic *getaną (“to find; to acquire, attain, get, hold, receive”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to find; to hold; to seize; to take”).
